sm: The show opens with headlines. President Trump has named Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, starting today, replacing Susie Wiles, who moves to his outside political operation. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called the choice awful. Trump is also meeting Dana White at the White House after joking about offering him the press secretary job. In Israel, President Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form a government, citing support from sixty-seven lawmakers against forty-six for Netanyahu. Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska remain very close, and Syria is reportedly preparing to send troops to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis. Legal Docket then introduces St. Mary Catholic Parish versus Roy, over Colorado's universal preschool tuition aid of about sixty-three hundred dollars per child, which requires schools to enroll families regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

The Archdiocese of Denver asks enrolling families to support church teaching, and the state barred its schools from the program. Lawyer Nicholas Reeves and two parents argue this burdens free exercise of religion. Colorado's lawyer, Helen Norton, says the rules apply equally, and more than forty faith-based preschools participate. The schools cite Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, and Carson. Justice Gorsuch suggested Colorado was trying to get around those cases, while Justice Kagan said they bar worse treatment, not better. Justice Kavanaugh raised the allowed preferences for vegetarian or Jewish schools. Justice Jackson said the case fits neither precedent bucket. Justice Sotomayor pressed on race and compared it to exclusions based on sexual practices.

Sotomayor's questions also touched the 303 Creative and Masterpiece Cakeshop cases and the Bob Jones University decision. Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, supporting the schools, said they only require parents to adhere to Catholic teaching. Justice Barrett asked how imposing a condition known to exclude certain schools differs from hostility. Colorado answered that no court found animus. Justice Alito asked about intent versus effect. Justice Kavanaugh asked why the state doesn't seek a win-win, noting that only thirty-four of about two thousand schools are Catholic. Colorado said location, cost and hours matter. Then the Monday Money Beat begins, with David Bahnsen on Thursday's sharp drop that erased about two and a half trillion dollars of market value.

Bahnsen says the Nasdaq fell five and a half percent Thursday, putting it in correction territory, but not yet a bear market. He says markets worry about AI spending and about the companies receiving that money, and that few understand how AI will make money. He doesn't think the election drove the swings, since divided government means nothing will get done. On affordability, he says Democrats ran on criticizing the president, not on a plan to lower prices. Senator Warren chairing the banking committee is mostly symbolic, though Democrats can block confirmations. On tariffs, he says Trump's policy is discretionary and hard to predict.

Bahnsen finishes by saying tariffs rest on one person's discretion, not legislation, so the new Congress changes little. Then The World History Book covers Ellis Island, closed seventy-two years ago after processing more than twelve million immigrants. Steerage passengers arrived for medical and legal inspection, and about two percent were turned away. At its peak in 1907, it processed over a million people. One story is of an Italian family whose daughter was sent back to Italy. After 1924 quota laws it became a detention center, and it closed in 1954. A five hundred million dollar campaign reopened it in the 1980s, and it now draws over three million visitors a year.
